Paragraph1: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
Paragraph2: "You should hang out more," I told Reva. "You'd like that, huh?" I could hear the whir of the machines in the background. "I gotta go, weirdo. I'm at the gym."On the morning of September 11, 2001, I went straight from the bodega where I got my coffee to Circuit City and charged a new TV/VCR combo on my Visa to record the news coverage. Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados. Everything was happening as it was supposed to. Reva was now "lost." For a full week I watched the same footage of the planes hitting the Twin Towers, the burning people plummeting, the buildings crumbling at the end like collapsing sand castles from every angle the news had to show.One woman leapt from a window from the North Tower and somehow caught my attention. She had on a skirt or a dress and was barefoot. As she spun, her stockings caught the updraft like sails, and I could see the outline of her thighs. She fell so gracefully. It looked almost like she was dancing. If I squinted, she looked like Reva. Of course I loved her—I had spent the last year mourning her as though she were dead. But I didn't cry. I wasn't hurt. I didn't feel sad. I just admired her, looked up at her there, so far above me and so elegant.

Paragraph1: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?
Paragraph2: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.

Paragraph1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
Paragraph2: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.

Paragraph1: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. I want to give Robbie and Cecilia what they lost out on in life. They both died because of a simple mistake which, although it grew in significance over the years, was not difficult to expunge. Or rather, I've always known the choice was mine. Was it right, however, to let them forgive? I've no doubt my fellow criminals are either behind bars or in important salaried positions. Hypocrites—I needed their praise and confirmation, and my sisters' doubts and contempt, in order to be cured. But now I must sleep. I will close my eyes and sleep. What purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on June 1, 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love? Who would want to believe that, except in the service of the bleakest realism? And what of that monstrous sister who systematically destroyed the love of her own sibling? I couldn't do it to them.
Paragraph2: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.

Paragraph1: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.
Paragraph2: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.

Paragraph1: A billionaire once invited me to lunch at his club in London. It was a grand place, but the billionaire wore skinny jeans, a hooded top, and designer trainers without a care in the world. He was very keen to show me his latest software project, which was a program that could predict which employees in a company would next betray their boss. I had to catch a plane immediately afterwards and so was a little restless, and he insisted on paying for my taxi to the airport, which was nice, since I'd come with a suitcase. We were supposed to be talking about a literary magazine he wanted to start, and I hadn't expected his personal security software to come up. But when we sat down and started, it was he who told me the story of his life. I assembled the biography: a humble beginning, the lessons in work and intellect, and finally this  tawny-haired and surprisingly well-muscled figure at the table across from me. I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money. He told me a lot more – about the complexity and immensity of his entrepreneurial schemes, such as a floating wind farm that would house and provide credit for its workers and thereby solve the problem of world poverty and ecocide; or another scheme he had for legally disposing of lawyers from people's personal lives. He also mentioned that he'd taken up playing drums in a rock band every Thursday night, because why not; and that he was presently expecting his eleventh child, counting the Guatemalan quadruplets he and his wife had adopted earlier. The billionaire talked for so long that I couldn’t keep up with it all, I was almost too exhausted to follow. Waitresses kept arriving, removing dishes and bringing huge plates of lobster and bottles of fine wine. His focus was so scattered, his enthusiasm so limitless, it was almost like that of a child. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, putting me in the taxi afterwards, though I didn't remember mentioning I was going there.
Paragraph2: The billionaire had invited me to lunch with him at a London club. When I arrived, I was surprised by how casually he dressed, in jeans and a white button-down. He was generous: on account of my enormous suitcase, he offered to call me a taxi to the airport when it was time to leave. He told me he was working on a software project that could predict an employee's capacity to betray their company. I didn't know why we were talking about this—we were meeting under the pretense of discussing a literary magazine that the billionaire was interested in starting—but I sat there and did my best to listen. He wanted to tell me many things, his whole life story. He had grown up poor, he said, but that hadn't lasted long, and now he had a floating windfarm that doubled as worker housing, and an idea for a scheme to keep lawyers out of people's personal business. He told me about the rock band he played drums in, and that he was expecting his eleventh child soon. This was in addition to the four Guatemalan quadruplets he had already adopted. It felt like too many children to me. I wondered if perhaps he thought that by creating this magazine, he might also fashion himself as a writer capable of being published in it. The idea seemed a stretch to me, but perhaps the billionaire was used to spanning such extreme logical leaps. The leap from man to billionaire was certainly larger than billionaire to writer. I was struggling to follow my own line of thinking. The waitress kept appearing, bringing brightly colored drinks and dishes that alternated between tasting too rich and too pungent. It had the opposite effect on the billionaire. Amidst the bright colors and flavors, the billionaire's face shone like a young boy who had been suddenly surrounded by mountains of his favorite sweets. When the food and drink had finally been swept away and the bill paid, he put me and my heavy suitcase in the taxi. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, which was a surprise. I hadn't recalled ever mentioning my destination.

Paragraph1: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.
Paragraph2: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.

Paragraph1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
Paragraph2: Look. I've been the one making the plan, and I want to be the one to execute it. There was a silence before she spoke again. I'll be honest, I'm not the kind of person who's so crazy about living that I want to put off dying as long as I possibly can. I'll be ready. In fact, I'm already impatient. But like I told you, no one can be sure how the cancer's going to behave. We all know there are sometimes surprises, and the body can be very stubborn about giving up, and it's always possible that treatment might be delayed. And I want this as natural as possible. I want to be in a certain state. I don't want to be in distress. I don't want to be rescued. I don't want my hand held. I'm sorry, but I just can't commit to any particular moment, any particular day. It could happen tomorrow. It could happen in a couple of weeks. As the saying goes, it'll be like the coming of the Lord. You won't know the day or the hour. But don't worry, she added, feeling the words catch in her throat. You'll know the minute afterward. Remembering my full mailbox, I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more. She pressed her lips together and frowned. I had gone too far. The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all. I'd rather you didn't mention the drug, or how I got it, to anyone. You understand, don't you? For your own protection—and for mine. But this promise I had already broken. I had already shared this information with someone.

Paragraph1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
Paragraph2: It must have been easier, in the late stages, not to have the story spilling directly into local news outlets. Easier to keep up the front. The Times erred only once, as far as one can tell, and described Walter as "arrogant" and "ethically compromised." Yet this dissonant portrait would not have resonated locally anyway, since Walter and Patty had already moved to Washington, D.C., about two years earlier. He'd gone to work for some energy-conservation organization after his youngest left college. It was hard to reconcile the full story with the optimistic, rural, green Walter who appeared to have been hampered and then corrupted by city life. Nowhere was the irony more poignant than back in St. Paul. The memory of the simple Walter, committed to punishing bad neighbors and raising good kids, stood in contrast to the fall of a man now willing to cut deals with big coal companies and ethically bend the rules in pursuit of his goals.To understand the derailment of Walter and Patty Berglund, one must remember those early years in Ramsey Hill when they were young pioneers in a neighborhood struggling to reclaim its nineteenth-century grandeur. The Berglunds bought their big Victorian for a song in 1990, when nobody wanted those properties because of broken windows, stray gunshots, and derelict urbanites holding out in rotting pillboxes. Walter and Patty invested time and sweat in their chosen project. They painted and fixed things, not merely as homeowners, but with the diligence of proselytizers converting neglected souls to middle-class potential. It was hard to miss Patty in those days—strolling down Laurel Avenue with a conspicuous brown stroller and her whipcord shoulders; she looked like the jock she claimed to be. She parked the shiny Subaru in sensible places and took the kids and cocker spaniel, Polly, to yoga classes and after-school programs out in the safer suburbs. Patty strengthened her household with Parks and Recreation and then afternoons of Wait Wait Don't Tell Me! followed by the zinfandel hour. At 10 p.m., after the kids were in bed, she was often seen stripping paint from woodwork or rehabbing furniture bought at local garage sales. She was benevolently juggling the old, the new, and the as-yet-unmade.

Paragraph1: I approach the hospital elevator. It is almost full up with nurses, doctors, and their patients. I slip myself between the heat of their bodies, which are all dressed in blue gowns or white coats. I press the button six. A voice comes on over a speaker hidden somewhere up above. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” the voice says. It repeats the words as the elevator whirs into motion and begins to rise. I wonder where in the building Dr. Y could be. I look down at the bag in my hands, admiring my fine craftsmanship–the softness of the leather, the straight, simple lines of my stitches. I have made it for the woman exactly to her specifications. It is undeniable. “Look,” I will say. “Look what I have made for you. See how beautiful it is?” I will offer it to her to try on. She will be grateful, of course, and in awe of the beauty of my hard work. She will try it on, adjusting the straps to her liking. She will arrange it this way and that: cross-body, or dangling from her fingers, or slung carelessly off the shoulder. “Do you trust me again?” I will ask. In the face of the beauty of the bag, she will have no choice but to say yes, to be nothing but thankful. And then, after she has given me her trust, I will take out my sheers and use them to cut out her heart. The heart and the bag will be mine alone to claim. My grip tightens on the sheers that I keep tucked behind the bag. The blades are long and sharp. They are a silver so bright that it flashes in the glare of the overhead elevator lighting when I sneak a look down at them. The elevator dings; we have arrived at the sixth floor.
Paragraph2: I was on my way to see the woman as a visitor, riding up in an elevator filled with doctors and nurses clutching clipboards, and patients doubled over in pain. "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine is needed in the consulting room," an announcement came over the PA system. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, however, never showed his face.My purpose in visiting her was clear enough: I intended to meet with her, regain her trust, and convince her to let me see the bag put to its intended use one last time."Would you mind undoing the ends of the cord so I can check how you attached it?" "Would you like me to take a photograph of you wearing it?" "Do you need to have another hole punched in the strap to make it longer?" I rehearsed these lines in my head. I realized I had never spoken to her so politely.In truth, I simply needed to make her put the bag down for a moment. I planned to face her, extend to her all the gratitude I felt for having been allowed to sew the bag on. Then, once she let her guard down, I would press the shears to her chest. The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries. The bag would be mine alone. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.
